name: Burncoat
headline: An old road north out of the city,
with stone walls at its side streets.
answer: Burncoat is a North Worcester neighborhood along Burncoat Street, a road the Massachusetts Historical Commission traces to a Native trail used as the Lancaster Way. The city's 1977-78 historic survey names Burncoat Street as one of the places of largest single-family house building between 1890 and 1950, and stone walls of about 1900 to 1910 still mark side-street entrances. Burncoat Park lies just north of I-290, and WRTA Route 14 runs on Burncoat Street.
meta: Burncoat, Worcester: the old Lancaster Way, the 1748 Amos Flagg House, stone walls of 1900-1910, the 1889 Burncoat Park and WRTA Route 14 on Burncoat Street.

boundaries.text: Burncoat has no official city boundary. Wikipedia lists it among the North Worcester neighborhoods; it follows Burncoat Street, whose National Register-listed Amos Flagg House (246 Burncoat Street) its article places in northeastern Worcester. Burncoat (North) Park lies just north of I-290 and Brittan Square, and the Burncoat Street Playground at 524 Burncoat Street, between Burncoat and West Boylston Streets, is the city's northernmost public park.

overview: Burncoat Street is older than the city around it. The Massachusetts Historical Commission's survey of Worcester infers a trail toward the Nashua River along its line before European settlement and records that Native trails stayed in use in the 17th century, with Burncoat Street serving as the Lancaster Way. The oldest building documented on the street is the Amos Flagg House at 246 Burncoat Street, a story-and-a-half timber-frame house with a side-gable roof and central chimney, probably built by Alan Flagg on a 50-acre parcel recorded in 1748 and listed on the National Register in 1980.

The farmland along the road gave way to houses in the decades around 1900. Preservation Worcester dates the mortared stone walls on the east side of Burncoat Street, from Thorndyke Road north to Devens Road, to between 1900 and 1910, built to mark the entrances to orchards and farms on Burncoat Plain; cast-in-place concrete piers flank each side street, and the walls now line residential streets that run parallel to the east. The survey behind Worcester's 1980 Multiple Resource Area nomination names Burncoat Street, with the city's west side, as the place of the largest expansion of single-family houses in the period it dates 1890 to 1950.

The city bought land for a park here in 1889. North Park, renamed Burncoat Park in 1910 according to Park Spirit of Worcester, gained Western Pond in 1898, the Boulder Bridge in 1901, a playground in 1926 and a hockey rink in 1930. In 1962 the Commonwealth took 8.2 acres of it for the I-290 expressway, and about 4 acres went to the school department for the Wawecus Road School, according to Park Spirit. Burncoat Street now carries WRTA Route 14 and holds Burncoat Middle School (135) and Burncoat High School (179), and a Burncoat/Greendale neighborhood meeting on the city's calendar in March 2025 was held at St. Michael's on-the-Heights, 340 Burncoat Street.

housing.text: The survey for Worcester's 1977-78 Multiple Resource Area National Register nomination names Burncoat Street, with the city's west side, as the place of the largest expansion of single-family houses between 1890 and 1950. Preservation Worcester records the 1900-1910 stone walls along Burncoat Street as entrances to former orchard and farm land on Burncoat Plain, with residential streets now running parallel to the east. No published count of housing types or ownership for Burncoat alone was found.

areas.name: Burncoat Street
areas.line: The neighborhood's spine and the old Lancaster Way, with the 1748 Amos Flagg House at 246, Burncoat Middle and High Schools at 135 and 179, St. Michael's on-the-Heights at 340 and the Burncoat Street Playground at 524; WRTA Route 14 runs its length.

areas.name: Burncoat Plain and the walled side streets
areas.line: Former orchard and farm land on the east side of Burncoat Street, where stone walls of about 1900 to 1910 with concrete piers mark each side street from Thorndyke Road north to Devens Road.

areas.name: Burncoat Park and North Parkway
areas.line: The 26-acre city park at 70 North Parkway, just north of I-290 and Brittan Square, with two ponds and the Wawecus Road School beside it at 20 Wawecus Road.

commute.text: Burncoat has no rail station; the nearest is Worcester station at Union Station, 2 Washington Square, downtown, on the MBTA Framingham/Worcester Line. WRTA Route 14 (Market32 and QCC via Burncoat Street) runs on Burncoat Street, and I-290 runs just south of Burncoat Park, which lost 8.2 acres to the expressway in 1962.

places.name: Burncoat (North) Park
places.line: A 26-acre city park at 70 North Parkway with two ponds (Western Pond was created in 1898), a baseball diamond, a multipurpose field and a sledding hill along Davidson Road with a 47-foot change in grade.

places.name: Amos Flagg House
places.line: A 1 1/2-story timber-frame colonial house at 246 Burncoat Street, probably built by Alan Flagg on a parcel recorded in 1748, with a side-gable roof, central chimney and clapboards; listed on the National Register on March 5, 1980.

places.name: Burncoat Street walls
places.line: Mortared stone walls with cast-in-place concrete piers along the east side of Burncoat Street from Thorndyke Road to Devens Road, built about 1900 to 1910 and profiled by Preservation Worcester as an endangered structure.

places.name: Burncoat Street Playground
places.line: A 1.2-acre city park at 524 Burncoat Street, between Burncoat and West Boylston Streets and the northernmost public park in Worcester, with a playground and basketball, volleyball and tennis courts (the tennis court doubles for pickleball).

places.name: Boulder Bridge
places.line: A bridge built in 1901 in Burncoat Park, which stood between the park's ponds before I-290 was built.

history.text: Native trails stayed in use, with Burncoat Street serving as the Lancaster Way, according to the Massachusetts Historical Commission.
The parcel on which the Amos Flagg House at 246 Burncoat Street stands was sold or mortgaged to Jonas Gale; the house was probably built by Alan Flagg.
The city bought 39.42 acres for what became Burncoat (North) Park.
The Commonwealth took 8.2 acres of Burncoat Park for the I-290 expressway.

search_notes: Exact-ranking queries for 'Burncoat Worcester real estate' and 'moving to Burncoat Worcester' were not run. Research searches for the neighborhood returned an Apartments.com Burncoat page, Redfin and Trulia listing and street pages, the Amos Flagg House article and the city's park pages. No sourced guide ties the Lancaster Way, the Burncoat Street walls, the park's history and the street's single-family development together, which is the gap this page fills.

faq.q: What is the median home price in Burncoat, Worcester?
faq.a: The Warren Group does not report Burncoat separately. Citywide, the median single-family sale price in Worcester for calendar year 2025 was $430,000 across 884 sales, up from $420,000 across 904 sales in 2024, according to its MA December 2025 Sales, Prices by Town report.

faq.q: Is there commuter rail near Burncoat?
faq.a: Burncoat has no station of its own. The nearest is Worcester station at Union Station, 2 Washington Square, downtown, on the MBTA Framingham/Worcester Line. WRTA Route 14 runs on Burncoat Street.

Worcester Public Schools, which has Burncoat Middle School (135 Burncoat Street), Burncoat High School (179 Burncoat Street) and the Wawecus Road School (20 Wawecus Road) in the area. School assignment is by address and is set by the district; review the district's profile with DESE.

faq.q: What kind of housing is in Burncoat?
faq.a: The city's 1977-78 historic survey names Burncoat Street as one of the two areas of largest single-family house building in Worcester between 1890 and 1950, on land that Preservation Worcester describes as former orchards and farms on Burncoat Plain.
At 70 North Parkway, just north of I-290 and Brittan Square. The 26-acre city park has two ponds, a baseball diamond, a multipurpose field and a sledding hill along Davidson Road.

notes: Written 2026-10-23. Boundaries: no official city boundary for Burncoat was found. Wikipedia's neighborhood list (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neighborhoods_in_Worcester,_Massachusetts) places Burncoat in North Worcester but names no streets; the boundary text is built from the Amos Flagg House article ('northeastern Worcester'), the city's Burncoat (North) Park page ('just north of I-290 and Brittan Square') and the Burncoat Street Playground page ('northern most public park', between Burncoat and West Boylston Streets, fairly close to Kendrick Field). Neither city park page names a neighborhood; they are included on the strength of the Burncoat name and their Burncoat Street and North Parkway locations. Lake Quinsigamond: the task suggested Burncoat is near the lake's north end, but no source found ties Burncoat to the lake (Wikipedia's lake article says only that an I-290 bridge crosses its north end; the city's Lake Park page does not mention Burncoat), so the lake was left out. Lancaster Way: from the MHC town report (https://www.sec.state.ma.us/divisions/mhc/preservation/survey/town-reports/wor.pdf), Contact Period (trail 'inferred from the Nashua River (Burncoat Street)') and Plantation Period ('Native trails continue in use, with the Lancaster Way (Burncoat Street)'). The origin of the name Burncoat was not found in any source opened and is not stated. Amos Flagg House: Wikipedia ('built about 1748'; 'probably built by Alan Flagg, on a 50-acre parcel sold or mortgaged to Jonas Gale in 1748'; NRHP March 5, 1980), with the NPGallery record (https://npgallery.nps.gov/AssetDetail/26b0e6aa-bc04-47a6-92ee-b6b0a6873aa6) confirming 246 Burncoat St and 1748. Single-family expansion: the OCR text of the Worcester Multiple Resource Area nomination (survey March 1977 to March 1978), Item 7 page 4, 1890-1950 section: 'The largest expansion of single-family houses occurred on the city's west side' and along Burncoat Street. Walls: Preservation Worcester's endangered-structures profile PDF (footer dated 2024; it notes earlier list appearances for other entries); the year the walls were first listed was not confirmed. A 2023 Telegram list (via AOL) names '227 Burncoat St.' among pillars and monuments added that year; whether that is the walls was not confirmed, so it was not used. Burncoat Park: the city page gives 26.0 acres, the 1889 purchase of 39.42 acres from five named owners, Western Pond 1898, Boulder Bridge 1901, skating 1923, playground 1926, hockey rink 1930 and the 1962 taking of 8.2 acres; Park Spirit of Worcester (https://parkspirit.org/parks/burncoat-park/) gives the 1910 renaming from North Park, a purchase year of 1888 (the city's 1889 is used), a current size of 16.4 acres (the city's 26.0 is used) and the Boulder Bridge's location between the ponds before I-290; whether the bridge still stands was not confirmed, so the place line says only where it stood. Schools: addresses from the district's school pages (https://www.worcesterschools.org/o/bms/, /o/bhs/, /o/wrs/); naming them does not imply assignment, which is by address and set by the district. The March 13, 2025 Burncoat/Greendale meeting at St. Michael's on-the-Heights, 340 Burncoat St, is from a city police calendar entry (https://www.worcesterma.gov/node/46420). WRTA Route 14 from https://www.therta.com/routes/. Left out: the Odd Fellows' Home (40 Randolph Rd, demolished) and the Chadwick-Brittan House (309 Lincoln St), because no source places them in Burncoat; Brittan Square's naming was not confirmed. Market null: the Warren Group PDF lists Worcester only as a citywide row; the FAQ figures repeat the citywide row recorded in the Grafton Hill and Greendale records (2024: 904 sales, $420,000; 2025: 884 sales, $430,000); the PDF was not re-read this session. School assignment is by address and set by the district. Fair housing: Preservation Worcester's phrase 'a quiet residential neighborhood' was not repeated (it characterizes the area); the walls are described by location and construction only. No wording describes residents.
